item.title: What’s Gavin McKenna’s Biggest Challenge in His First NHL Season?
item.dc:creator: Old Prof
item.description:
The post What’s Gavin McKenna’s Biggest Challenge in His First NHL Season? appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.

Gavin McKenna is adjusting to the NHL, while Jim Hiller faces a balancing act with the young Maple Leafs prospect's ice time.

The post What’s Gavin McKenna’s Biggest Challenge in His First NHL Season? appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.
item.content:encoded:
The post What’s Gavin McKenna’s Biggest Challenge in His First NHL Season? appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.

During the off-season, the Toronto Maple Leafs were fortunate enough to win the draft lottery and select Gavin McKenna first overall. He’s a young player. He’s just learning his way around the NHL. It hasn’t been easy for him. He said it’s been hard to adjust to the demands of the NHL game. Part of that is sitting. And he’s not used to that. As he’s sitting there chomping at the bit, how does he stay engaged? That’s a big question. In a recent interview, he talked about that exact issue.

McKenna Shares How He’s Tried to Become a Better NHL Player

McKenna was recently interviewed about the chances he’s been given and how he’s trying to build his game. In the same interview, Coach Jim Hiller also had a chance to talk about how he’s worked with the youngster, particularly given the game circumstances and the ice time he’s getting. What does the coach expect of McKenna, and what does the player expect of himself?

During his interview, McKenna talked about three things. First, how does he stay in the game when he’s not playing very many minutes? How does he stay locked in?

McKenna noted that “It’s tough to stay in it and find ways to get going on that next shift. But for me, I think being dialled in, watching the game and watching plays happen, really keeps me dialled in.”

He also spoke about how he’s trying to make the most of his limited chances. He said touching the puck becomes harder when he’s playing less, so he has to be more deliberate.

As he noted, “When I’m out there on that next shift, I just try to be around the puck a lot more. You know, it’s going to be harder to come by puck touches when you’re not playing as much. So for me, trying to be around it and get those touches will be key.”

Finally, McKenna talked about working on his defensive game because he wants to see improvement in that area, as he noted,

“I think defensively it’s gotten a little bit better. I find we’re not hemmed in our zone as much anymore, and we’re starting to play in the O-zone a little bit more. That’s something I’ve been wanting to work on, and I’ve found it’s coming a little bit more. So I want to keep building on that, and hopefully being in the O-zone more leads to a couple more goals.”

Coach Jim Hiller Shares How He’s Trying to Manage McKenna’s Ice Time

Hiller spoke about the balancing act coaches face when managing a young player’s ice time. He considers McKenna’s performance, the score, and each game’s circumstances.

As Hiller noted,

“It’s just a balancing act. I think different nights, just like any other player, different nights you’re having a good night, you should probably play more, right? Then there are other circumstances where maybe you’re not going as well, or the score is that you’re trailing or you’re leading. So there are a number of different variables that go into it, and it goes on a night-to-night basis.”

The Bottom Line for McKenna’s Adjustment

McKenna is learning that playing in the NHL is much more than having elite hockey skills. He also has to stay mentally engaged and learn everything that happens on the ice. In some ways, it’s a much different game from what he’s played before. It’s still hockey, but it requires different skills.

As a coach, Hiller has to consider what’s best for the team and the development of his elite young prospect. Putting all that together is difficult. What’s the right balance? That’s the question as McKenna learns to play in the NHL as a rookie.

item.title: Hyman’s Comments Raise an Interesting Question About the Oilers’ Coach
item.dc:creator: Old Prof
item.description:
The post Hyman’s Comments Raise an Interesting Question About the Oilers’ Coach appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.

Zach Hyman remembers Mike Babcock as more than a coach. His experience raises an interesting question about the Oilers bench boss.

The post Hyman’s Comments Raise an Interesting Question About the Oilers’ Coach appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.
item.content:encoded:
The post Hyman’s Comments Raise an Interesting Question About the Oilers’ Coach appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.

In a recent interview, Zach Hyman spoke about his relationship with Mike Babcock, the Edmonton Oilers’ head coach. What’s interesting is that Babcock coached Hyman with the Toronto Maple Leafs when Hyman was a young player. As you can hear in the interview, Hyman believes Babcock had a huge impact on his career.

How Did Babcock Impact Hyman as a Young Maple Leafs Player?

Here are Hyman’s thoughts:

You always need somebody who believes in you, especially early in your career, when you’re trying to make a name for yourself and grab a roster spot. And he was somebody who believed in me right from the start. There were a lot of doubters in Toronto early on about whether I should have been playing where I was, but he always had the confidence to put me on the ice, trust my game, and help me grow as a player.

In fact, Babcock used to say Hyman was the hardest worker and best puck digger on the team. That had a lot of impact on Hyman because it boosted his confidence as a young player. Given Babcock’s reputation, it’s interesting to hear someone speak so highly of him.

As Hyman noted, you always grow as a person. He’s not the same person he was six or seven years ago, so he’s been great. Obviously, the record speaks for itself in the hockey department, but personally, he’s been phenomenal.

The Oilers’ Players Are Enjoying Being Around Babcock

Hyman thinks the guys have really enjoyed being around him, getting to know him. He’s obviously known him for a long time, but he’s brought in that new light to the locker room. And, as Hyman says, “You know, you’ve been around, you’ve seen it. It’s been very positive, so it’s been great.”

Hyman sees Babcock as more than just a coach. Babcock was also a significant mentor to him as a person. Their relationship meant he pushed him as a coach but also helped him grow. Hyman believes that Babcock believed in him when others doubted him. That must have had a real impact on a young player and helped build his confidence.

Sure, Hyman came in with the skills. But he had to figure out how to put them together; Babcock helped him. What do we take away from all this? Babcock has had different impacts on other people.

Hyman Has Enjoyed His Second Go-Round with Babcock

And, yeah, it’s been really fun having a second stint with him, being older now. Everything goes… like, 24 when we started, and now I’m 34. So I think everybody knows how highly I think of him, and it’s been a great start here in Edmonton.

So far, Babcock’s work with the team seems positive. How does that change the way we see Babcock in his current role?

Babcock has done some questionable things in his life, but he has certainly made an impact on this young player. How do we think of him? That’s the big question now: can he help the Edmonton Oilers reach the success that they’ve needed?

item.title: Chris Kreider Injury Timeline Revealed, and It’s a Blow for Montreal
item.dc:creator: NHL Trade Talk
item.description:
The post Chris Kreider Injury Timeline Revealed, and It’s a Blow for Montreal appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.

The Montreal Canadiens will be without forward Chris Kreider for the next 6-8 weeks. He is out with an injury.

The post Chris Kreider Injury Timeline Revealed, and It’s a Blow for Montreal appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.
item.content:encoded:
The post Chris Kreider Injury Timeline Revealed, and It’s a Blow for Montreal appeared first on NHL Trade Talk.

The Montreal Canadiens will be without forward Chris Kreider for the next 6-8 weeks. The Canadiens confirmed the news Saturday, hours before Montreal was set to host the Colorado Avalanche. Kreider suffered a lower-body injury in Thursday’s 5-2 win over Boston, and the team confirmed the extended absence.

The injury is a blow to Montreal’s forward depth. Kreider has three goals and nine points through 19 games this season, along with 22 shots on net, eight blocked shots and 21 hits.

With Kreider out, RotoWire suggests youngsters Florian Xhekaj and Owen Beck could compete for the vacated playing time. Montreal will count on that pair to help fill the void while Kreider recovers.

The positive here is that some thought Kreider’s injury looked like it was going to be much more serious, thinking he could be gone for the season and had a torn MCL or ACL. As bad as the timeline is, one could argue this is actually very good news.
